misconceptions.statement: If A takes 10 days and B takes 15 days, together they take 25 days.
misconceptions.why: Students add the numbers they see, as in whole-number addition, without asking what the numbers mean.
misconceptions.fix: Days cannot be added; the daily work is added. A does 1/10 and B does 1/15 per day, so together 1/6 per day, which means 6 days.

probe.question: A can do a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. In how many days will they finish it together?

misconceptions.root_belief: just add the numbers given in the problem
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of proportional reasoning errors in rate problems

misconceptions.statement: Working together, two people take the average of their individual times.
misconceptions.why: Students feel the combined time must lie between the two times, so they average them.
misconceptions.fix: Two workers together are faster than either alone, so the time is less than the smaller of the two times. Add the daily rates to find it.

probe.question: A takes 12 days and B takes 6 days alone. How long together?

misconceptions.root_belief: a combined result lies between the parts

misconceptions.statement: A and B together take 1/10 + 1/15 days.
misconceptions.why: Students stop after adding the rates and forget that the sum is work per day, not days.
misconceptions.fix: 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 is the work done in one day. The time is the reciprocal, 6 days.

probe.question: A does a job in 10 days, B in 15 days. State the days they need together.

misconceptions.root_belief: the last number computed is the final answer

misconceptions.statement: The whole work has to be given as a number like 100 or the number of workers.
misconceptions.why: Word problems often mention numbers of units, so students think the work needs a count.
misconceptions.fix: When the amount of work is not given, take the whole job as 1 (or any convenient number such as the LCM of days) and work consistently.

probe.question: A can paint a wall in 8 days. What fraction does A paint in one day?
probe.wrong_answer: Cannot be found, since the amount of work is not given

misconceptions.root_belief: a quantity must be given a number to be used

misconceptions.statement: If a person takes 8 days, the work done in one day is 8.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the number of days with the amount of work per day.
misconceptions.fix: The whole work done in 8 days means one day's share is 1/8 of the work.

probe.question: A finishes a task in 5 days. How much of the task does A finish in 1 day?

misconceptions.root_belief: the number in the problem is the rate itself
misconceptions.source_hint: research on rate and ratio reasoning showing confusion of time and rate

misconceptions.statement: The person who takes more days does more work each day.
misconceptions.why: Students link bigger numbers with bigger effect.
misconceptions.fix: More days for the same job means less work each day. 1/12 per day is less than 1/8 per day.

probe.question: A takes 12 days and B takes 8 days for the same job. Who does more work in a day?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger number means bigger effect
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of inverse relationships in rate problems

misconceptions.statement: If a person does 1/4 of the work in a day, the job takes 1/4 days.
misconceptions.why: Students carry the fraction directly into the answer without inverting.
misconceptions.fix: If one day gives 1/4 of the job, the whole job needs 4 days, the reciprocal of 1/4.

probe.question: A does 1/6 of a job every day. How many days for the whole job?

misconceptions.root_belief: the number given is the number asked

misconceptions.statement: If A does 1/10 of the work per day, in 4 days A has done 1/10 + 4 of the work.
misconceptions.why: Students don't connect repeated daily work with multiplication of fractions.
misconceptions.fix: Work done = daily rate times days = 4 × 1/10 = 2/5 of the work.

probe.question: A can complete a job in 10 days. How much is done in 4 days?

misconceptions.root_belief: combine the numbers with any operation that looks right

misconceptions.statement: If 5 workers take 12 days, then 10 workers will take 24 days.
misconceptions.why: Students think more workers and more days go up together because both numbers are doubled in other direct-proportion problems.
misconceptions.fix: More workers finish the same work in fewer days; doubling workers halves the days, so 6 days.

probe.question: 5 workers finish a job in 12 days. How many days will 10 workers take?

misconceptions.root_belief: more of one thing always means more of another
misconceptions.source_hint: research on direct vs inverse proportion confusion in school students

misconceptions.statement: If 6 workers take 10 days, then 3 workers take 5 days, since fewer workers need fewer days.
misconceptions.why: Students halve both quantities because of the idea that less of one means less of the other.
misconceptions.fix: Half the workers take twice as long: 20 days. Workers and days change in opposite directions for fixed work.

probe.question: 6 workers complete a job in 10 days. How many days will 3 workers need?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule that worked before works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on proportional reasoning showing additive and direct-proportion overuse

misconceptions.statement: Doubling the work with the same workers does not change the time.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the number of workers staying same and ignore the amount of work.
misconceptions.fix: With the same workers, twice the work takes twice the time, since work and time are directly proportional.

probe.question: 4 men build a wall in 6 days. How long will the same 4 men take for a wall twice as long?

misconceptions.root_belief: only the changed-looking quantity matters

misconceptions.statement: If 3 men take 8 days, then 4 men take 8 - 1 = 7 days.
misconceptions.why: Students use additive thinking: one more worker means one day less.
misconceptions.fix: Total man-days is 3 × 8 = 24, so 4 men take 24 ÷ 4 = 6 days. The change is multiplicative, not additive.

probe.question: 3 men finish a job in 8 days. How many days will 4 men take?

misconceptions.root_belief: changes are always by adding or subtracting the same amount
misconceptions.source_hint: research on additive vs multiplicative reasoning in proportion tasks

misconceptions.statement: If 4 men work 5 days and then 2 days are left to finish, extra men are not needed since man-days is not important.
misconceptions.why: Students treat each day separately and do not see work as men times days.
misconceptions.fix: Work is measured as men × days. The same total man-days is needed however the men are arranged over the days.

probe.question: A job needs 40 man-days. 5 men have worked 4 days. How many man-days are left?

misconceptions.root_belief: only the time counts, not the amount of effort

misconceptions.statement: A worker who is twice as efficient takes twice as many days.
misconceptions.why: Students link 'twice' to the days directly, ignoring that efficiency and time are opposite.
misconceptions.fix: A worker twice as efficient does the same job in half the time.

probe.question: B is twice as efficient as A. A takes 20 days. How long does B take?

misconceptions.root_belief: twice as much means twice the number
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of misreading comparative language in ratio problems

misconceptions.statement: If A takes 6 days and B takes 9 days, A's and B's efficiencies are in ratio 6:9.
misconceptions.why: Students write the ratio of the numbers given without checking what is being compared.
misconceptions.fix: Efficiency is in the inverse ratio of days, so A:B = 1/6 : 1/9 = 3:2.

probe.question: A takes 6 days, B takes 9 days for a job. What is the ratio of their efficiencies A:B?

misconceptions.root_belief: ratio of given numbers is the ratio asked
misconceptions.source_hint: research on inverse proportion errors in ratio problems

misconceptions.statement: If A and B work together for 2 days and then A leaves, the remaining work is found by taking away 2 days from the total days.
misconceptions.why: Students subtract days instead of subtracting fractions of work.
misconceptions.fix: Find work done as 2 × (combined rate), subtract from 1, and then divide by the remaining worker's rate.

probe.question: A and B together do 1/6 of a job daily. After 2 days, how much work is left?

misconceptions.root_belief: days can be used as the amount of work

misconceptions.statement: An outlet pipe also adds to the filling, so all pipes' rates are added.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the rule 'add rates' from combined work and ignore the opposite effect of a leak.
misconceptions.fix: A pipe that empties works against filling, so its rate is subtracted: net rate = inlet rate − outlet rate.

probe.question: A pipe fills a tank in 6 h and a drain empties it in 12 h. What fraction fills in 1 hour when both are open?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on negative quantities in rate word problems

misconceptions.statement: A tank has a pipe that fills it in 4 hours and a leak that empties it in 4 hours, so it fills in 8 hours.
misconceptions.why: Students think the two effects add up because both take the same time.
misconceptions.fix: Equal rates cancel: net rate is 0, so the tank never fills.

probe.question: An inlet fills a tank in 4 h and an outlet empties it in 4 h. How long to fill with both open?

misconceptions.root_belief: opposing effects still add up

misconceptions.statement: With both pipes open, the tank always gets filled, whatever the outlet's speed.
misconceptions.why: Students expect the inlet to win since the problem asks about filling.
misconceptions.fix: If the outlet empties faster than the inlet fills, the net rate is negative and the tank empties instead.

probe.question: An inlet fills a tank in 10 h and an outlet empties it in 5 h. What happens when both are opened?

misconceptions.root_belief: the expected outcome in the question always happens

misconceptions.statement: If an inlet takes 6 h and outlet takes 10 h, the tank fills in 6 − 10 hours.
misconceptions.why: Students subtract the time values instead of the rates.
misconceptions.fix: Subtract the rates, 1/6 − 1/10 = 1/15, so the tank fills in 15 hours.

probe.question: Inlet fills a tank in 6 h and outlet empties it in 10 h. Time to fill with both open?

misconceptions.root_belief: just combine the numbers given in the problem

misconceptions.statement: If two people work together on a job, the money is always shared equally.
misconceptions.why: Students think teamwork means equal reward regardless of each person's contribution.
misconceptions.fix: Wages are divided in the ratio of work each did, which depends on rate and days worked.

probe.question: A and B finish a job together. A did 3/5 of the work and B did 2/5. They get Rs 500. What is A's share?

misconceptions.root_belief: fair means everyone gets the same

misconceptions.statement: Wages are shared in the ratio of the days each person takes alone.
misconceptions.why: Students use the numbers given directly as the ratio, without noting that more days alone means slower work.
misconceptions.fix: Wages follow the work done, which is the inverse ratio of days alone when they work together for the same time. If A takes 10 days and B 15, the ratio is 3:2.

probe.question: A alone takes 10 days and B alone 15 days. They work together and earn Rs 500. A's share?

misconceptions.root_belief: ratio of given numbers is the ratio asked
misconceptions.source_hint: research on inverse proportion errors in ratio problems

misconceptions.statement: If two people work the same number of days, they must get the same wage.
misconceptions.why: Students equate time spent with work done, ignoring the speed difference.
misconceptions.fix: The faster worker does more work in the same days, so earns more when paid by work done.

probe.question: A does 1/10 of a job and B does 1/15 per day, both work 5 days and are paid by work done. Do they get equal wages?

misconceptions.root_belief: time spent equals amount achieved
